What survives: steps in the correct order

The surviving text explains that a solution is written as steps in the correct order. This prevents errors during problem solving, and anyone can understand and use the steps easily. Computers also follow step-by-step instructions (Fig 2.2), and good planning leads to correct results.

blocks.title: Decomposition (from the chapter summary)
blocks.text: Decomposition is the process of breaking a large or complex problem into smaller, manageable parts.

blocks.title: Algorithm (from the chapter summary)
blocks.text: An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions used to solve a problem or perform a task.

blocks.alt: A flowchart from top to bottom: an oval Start, then boxes 1 Boil water, 2 Steep the tea, 3 Add milk or lemon, 4 Serve the tea, then an oval End, joined by downward arrows. A key on the left reads oval: start or end, box: one step, arrow: what comes next. A note on the right says each step is clear, the order matters (serving before boiling gives the wrong result), and a computer follows instructions the same way.
blocks.caption: An algorithm for making tea (original flowchart after Fig 2.2).
blocks.long_description: A flowchart is one way of writing an algorithm. Swapping two steps changes the result, which is why the order must be planned.

blocks.text: Problem-solving steps in the chapter's exercise

items: Identify the problem: the exercise gives this as the first step of problem solving.
Break the problem into smaller parts (decomposition).
Write the solution as an algorithm: clear steps in the correct order.
Evaluate and improve the solution (the next lesson).

blocks.explanation: Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller parts that can be solved one at a time. Example: making a school result sheet can be split into collecting marks, adding each student's total, working out percentages and grades, and printing the sheet; each part is simple, and together they solve the whole problem.
